templates.name: Hypothetical finding supports or weakens a single claim (causal, comparison, existence, generalization, prediction)
Hypothetical finding discriminates between competing explanations (support or weaken)
Quotation from a literary work illustrates a claim (single trait, two-part, contrast)
Quotation from a person (participant, respondent, historian, critic, article) supports or challenges a claim
Data completion: lookup (one cell or bar, reverse lookup, filter)
Data completion: extreme or rank (max/min, possibly after a filter)
Data completion: pairwise comparison (one or two comparisons)
Data completion: passage criterion or presence/absence combined with the display
Data description: trend or change over time supports a conclusion
Data description: condition vs control or group comparison supports a conclusion
Data description: quantified claim (for each, all except one)
Data description: multi-part, interaction, or passage-plus-data claim

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (learned cue; the key supplies the missing premise that the sound alone draws the seals when no food is present)
items.passage: Acoustic tags, devices that emit regular pulses of sound, are routinely attached to wild fish so that researchers can monitor the fish’s movements, but these pulses fall within the hearing range of several marine predators. Amanda Stansbury, Vincent Janik, and colleagues presented ten captive grey seals (Halichoerus grypus) with repeated foraging trials in which each seal investigated twenty boxes: one contained a fish carrying a tag, another contained an untagged fish, and the remainder were empty. Across successive trials, the seals located the tagged fish after inspecting progressively fewer other boxes. The researchers claim that the seals had learned to interpret the tag’s sound itself as an indication of food.
items.stem: Which finding from Stansbury, Janik, and colleagues’ study, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ claim?
options: Over the course of the trials, the seals needed less and less time to locate both the box holding the tagged fish and the box holding the untagged fish.
When the box holding the tagged fish was placed in a new position, the seals usually searched first at the spot where that box had been in the previous trial.
In trials with a tag in one box and no fish in any box, the seals found the box with the tag sooner than an otherwise identical box without one.
The seals that were quickest to reach the box holding the tagged fish took no less time than the other seals did to pull the fish out once they had reached it.
items.explanation: The researchers claim that “the seals had learned to interpret the tag’s sound itself as an indication of food.” In the main trials the tag was always attached to a fish, so the seals might have been drawn by the fish rather than by the sound. If the seals went to a box holding only a tag sooner than to an identical box without one, when no fish was present anywhere, the sound alone was drawing them, which is what interpreting it as an indication of food means. Choice C therefore supports the claim.

A.recipe: TRAP: general improvement at the task, consistent with any cue
A.why_wrong: Getting faster at finding both fish shows only that the seals learned the task; it would happen whether they used the tag’s sound, smell, or memory, so it does not show that the sound itself signaled food.

B.recipe: OPP: points to spatial memory instead of sound
B.why_wrong: Searching where the tagged fish used to be suggests the seals relied on remembering a location, not on the tag’s sound, so it would weaken rather than support the claim.

D.recipe: OFF: same seals, different variable (handling time)
D.why_wrong: How quickly seals removed a fish from a box concerns their handling skill, not whether the tag’s sound guided them to food.

sources.what: Stansbury, Götz, Deecke, Janik 2015, Proc. R. Soc. B 282: 20141595: ten grey seals each searched 20 foraging boxes in 20 trials, one box with a tagged fish, one with an untagged fish, the rest empty; the tagged box was found after fewer non-tag box visits across trials; in a control with a tag in one box and no fish in any box, the tagged box was found significantly faster than the control box; the seals learn to use tag sounds as an indicator of food location

items.notes: Band-7 moves: the claim (sound as a food signal) needs the unstated premise that the sound alone, without any fish, attracts the seals; the key is the study’s own tag-only control. A TRAP (improvement on both boxes, true in the study and consistent with any cue), B OPP (spatial memory), D OFF (handling time). Steps: in the main trials the tag and fish always co-occur; so a tag-only test is needed; the key reports that test. The second control (inaccessible fish pieces in the empty boxes) was left out to keep a single key.
band7_moves: key supplies the missing premise (sound alone attracts with no food present)
TRAP distractor consistent with every cue (faster at both boxes)
stem names the study and the claimant

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (indirect effect; the key supplies the premise that the killed predator limits the pest)
items.passage: DEET and picaridin, the active ingredients in many insect repellents, wash off skin and enter ponds and streams through wastewater. Rafael Almeida, Emma Rosi, and colleagues at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York exposed larval mosquitoes and larval spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum), major predators of mosquito larvae, to concentrations of these compounds like those found in surface waters. Neither repellent harmed the mosquito larvae, and DEET did not harm the salamanders, but between 45 and 65 percent of the salamander larvae exposed to picaridin died within 25 days. The researchers suggest that picaridin in ponds could therefore lead to more adult mosquitoes.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ suggestion?
options: In ponds with spotted salamander larvae, far fewer mosquito larvae survived to become adults than in similar ponds without the salamanders.
Female mosquitoes tend to avoid laying their eggs in water that contains picaridin, depositing them instead in nearby water that contains no repellent.
Salamander larvae exposed to DEET grew and developed at about the same rate as salamander larvae that were not exposed to any repellent.
Salamander larvae that survived exposure to picaridin were, by the end of the study, about the same size as larvae that had not been exposed.
items.explanation: The researchers suggest that “picaridin in ponds could therefore lead to more adult mosquitoes.” The passage shows that picaridin kills salamander larvae but not mosquito larvae; for that to mean more mosquitoes, the salamanders must actually keep mosquito numbers down. If far fewer mosquito larvae become adults where salamander larvae are present, then losing the salamanders to picaridin would let more mosquitoes survive, so choice A supports the suggestion.

B.recipe: OPP: fewer mosquitoes where picaridin is present
B.why_wrong: If mosquitoes avoid laying eggs in water with picaridin, ponds containing it would produce fewer mosquitoes, which weakens rather than supports the suggestion.

C.recipe: TRAP: true of the wrong repellent
C.why_wrong: DEET is not the compound that killed the salamanders, so how DEET-exposed larvae grew says nothing about whether picaridin’s effect on salamanders would increase mosquitoes.

D.why_wrong: The size of the surviving larvae does not show whether salamanders control mosquito numbers, which is the link the suggestion depends on.

sources.what: Almeida, Han, Reisinger, Kagemann, Rosi 2018, Biology Letters 14: 20180526: environmentally realistic concentrations of DEET and picaridin repellents; larval mosquitoes not affected by either; no salamander mortality in control and DEET treatments, 45 to 65% mortality in picaridin treatments after 25 days; picaridin may increase adult mosquito abundance owing to decreased predation pressure; study at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies, Millbrook, New York

items.notes: Larval salamanders are named in the paper as a major predator of mosquito larvae; species Ambystoma maculatum and Cary Institute location from the full text (PMC6227861). Steps: picaridin kills the predator but not the prey; the suggestion needs the unstated premise that the predator limits the prey; the key supplies it. Wrong options: B OPP, C true-of-the-other-compound TRAP, D OFF.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates between explanations (large-scale burning vs small-scale farming; charcoal record)
items.passage: Some researchers have argued that farmers of the Kuahuqiao culture, who grew rice on China’s Ningshao Plain roughly 8,000 years ago, cleared land by burning large areas of vegetation. To test this idea, geoscientists from Nanjing University examined charcoal particles preserved in sediment cores collected near the Kuahuqiao site. Combustion experiments had shown that charcoal from herbaceous plants, such as grasses, forms elongated particles, whereas charcoal from wood forms shorter, blockier ones, so particle shape indicates which kind of vegetation burned. The team concluded that Kuahuqiao agriculture was limited in extent and did not depend on large-scale slash-and-burn clearing.
items.stem: Which finding about the sediment cores, if true, would most directly support the team’s conclusion?
options: During the Kuahuqiao period, a larger share of the charcoal came from woody plants than in earlier layers, consistent with the burning of trees and shrubs near the settlement.
Charcoal from herbaceous plants became much more abundant around the time rice farming began and reached its highest levels during the Kuahuqiao period.
Layers dating to the Kuahuqiao period contain phytoliths, microscopic silica bodies, from cultivated rice, while earlier layers contain phytoliths from wild grasses only.
Less charcoal of any kind accumulated during the Kuahuqiao period than during the centuries before the culture appeared, indicating less intense fires.
items.explanation: The team concluded that “Kuahuqiao agriculture was limited in extent and did not depend on large-scale slash-and-burn clearing.” If farmers had burned large areas of land, the cores should hold more charcoal from the Kuahuqiao period than from before it. A drop in charcoal of every kind, showing that fires became less intense once the culture appeared, is what the team’s view predicts and the rival view does not, so choice D supports the conclusion.

A.why_wrong: A larger share of woody charcoal shows only that wood made up more of what burned; it says nothing about how much burned in total, so it is consistent with large-scale clearing as well as with small-scale farming.

B.why_wrong: A sharp rise in charcoal from burned grasses and other plants when rice farming began would point to widespread burning, supporting the view the team rejects.

C.recipe: OFF: shows farming, not its scale or method
C.why_wrong: Rice phytoliths would show that rice was grown during the Kuahuqiao period, but not whether land was cleared by large-scale burning.

sources.what: Hu, Zhou, Lu, Zhang, Min et al. 2020, PLoS ONE 15(8): e0237592 (Nanjing University): debate over slash-and-burn by Kuahuqiao rice farmers on the Ningshao Plain; combustion experiments show herbaceous charcoal has higher length-to-width ratios than woody charcoal; sediment cores near the Kuahuqiao site; during the Kuahuqiao period (8250 to 7450 yr BP) the relative abundance of woody charcoal increased but overall fire intensity decreased; farming restricted to a small area, large-scale slash-and-burn not adopted

items.notes: Discrimination check: the large-scale-burning view predicts more charcoal in the Kuahuqiao layers; the small-scale view predicts no rise. The key (less charcoal overall, the study’s actual result) splits them; A (more woody share, also the actual result) fits both; B is the rival’s prediction; C confirms farming only. Ages rounded to about 8,000 years ago.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates an indirect claim (early modern verse; vow of defiance and death’s effortless victory)
items.passage: “To the Dead in the Graveyard Underneath My Window” is a 1915 poem by Adelaide Crapsey. The bedridden speaker proclaims her refusal to imitate the motionless dead buried beneath her window, yet she intimates that death will overcome this resistance without any real exertion: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from “To the Dead in the Graveyard Underneath My Window” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “And if the many sayings of the wise / Teach of submission I will not submit / But with a spirit all unreconciled / Flash an unquenched defiance to the stars.”
“And in ironic quietude who is / The despot of our days and lord of dust / Needs but, scarce heeding, wait to drop / Grim casual comment on rebellion’s end;”
“My eyes may follow but my feet are held. / Recumbent as you others must I too / Submit? Be mimic of your movelessness / With pillow and counterpane for stone and sod?”
“And I would walk the road and I would be / Deep in the wooded shade and I would reach / The windy mountain tops that touch the clouds.”
items.explanation: The claim is that the speaker intimates “that death will overcome this resistance without any real exertion.” In choice B, “The despot of our days and lord of dust,” that is, death, “Needs but, scarce heeding, wait” to make a “Grim casual comment on rebellion’s end.” Death has only to wait, barely paying attention, for the speaker’s rebellion to end, which is what the claim describes.

A.recipe: HALF: the vow of defiance without death’s effortless victory
A.why_wrong: The speaker refuses to submit and promises “unquenched defiance,” but nothing in these lines suggests that death will end her defiance without effort.

C.why_wrong: The speaker says her “feet are held” and asks whether she must submit like the dead, which concerns her present confinement, not how easily death will end her defiance.

D.why_wrong: These lines express the speaker’s longing to walk the road and reach the mountain tops; they do not mention death or how it will deal with her defiance.

sources.what: Adelaide Crapsey, Verse (Rochester: Manas Press, 1915; Knopf printing, copyright 1915, 1922), poem “To the Dead in the Graveyard Underneath My Window,” subtitled “Written in a Moment of Exasperation,” dated Saranac Lake, N.Y. 1914; the preface notes her window overlooked the Saranac graveyard; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (double space before “Be” closed to one, straight apostrophe curled)

items.notes: Band-7 settings: early modernist verse; indirect claim verb (“intimates”); distractors are the same speaker in nearby states (defiance, confinement, longing). The final stanza’s quoted line (“Yes, yes. . . . Wilful and petulant but now / As dead and quiet as the others are.”) was left out because it would also illustrate the claim.
band7_moves: distractors are the same speaker in nearby emotions (defiance, confinement, longing)
key needs the figure (despot of our days, lord of dust) read as death

items.subtype: Data description: two-part claim with a difference of differences (richness up in both strata; diversity gap larger belowground)
items.passage: In southern Africa, cattle were once penned overnight in enclosures called kraals, and the accumulated dung enriches the soil for decades after a kraal is abandoned. Justice Muvengwi and colleagues sampled invertebrates on the ground surface and in the soil at twelve abandoned kraals in Zimbabwe’s Save Valley Conservancy and at nearby control plots. Besides counting species, they calculated the Shannon index, a diversity measure that increases with both the number of species and the evenness with which individuals are distributed among them. The researchers concluded that kraals increased species numbers in both habitats but had a much greater effect on diversity belowground than aboveground.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Muvengwi and colleagues’ conclusion?
options: Kraals had more species than control plots in both habitats, but their Shannon index exceeded that of control plots by more than twice as much belowground as aboveground.
Kraals had more species aboveground than belowground, while the Shannon index on kraals was nearly the same aboveground, at 1.89, as it was belowground, at 1.91.
Control plots had a higher Shannon index aboveground than belowground, and kraals had a higher Shannon index aboveground than control plots had aboveground.
Kraals had about 6 more species than control plots aboveground and about 5 more species than control plots belowground, so the kraals’ effect on the number of species was similar in the two habitats.

table.title: Invertebrate Species Richness and Diversity on Abandoned Kraals and Control Plots

items.explanation: The conclusion has two parts: the kraals “increased species numbers in both habitats” but “had a much greater effect on diversity belowground than aboveground.” Kraals had more species aboveground (15.83 against 9.92) and belowground (10.33 against 5.42). Their Shannon index exceeded the control plots’ by 0.66 belowground (1.91 against 1.25) but by only 0.27 aboveground (1.89 against 1.62), more than twice as large a difference. Choice A states both parts.

B.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison of the wrong cells (strata within kraals)
B.why_wrong: Both statements are accurate, but they compare the two habitats on kraals with each other; without the control plots they cannot show what difference the kraals made.

C.recipe: IRREL/PART: accurate cells, aboveground effect only
C.why_wrong: Both comparisons are accurate, but they never compare the kraals’ effect belowground with their effect aboveground, which is what the second part of the conclusion is about.

D.recipe: HALF: the species part only, with an inference about richness
D.why_wrong: The differences in species counts are accurate, but they concern only the number of species and say nothing about diversity, so they cannot support the claim that the kraals affected diversity far more in the soil.

sources.what: Muvengwi, Chikorowondo, Mbiba, Gandiwa 2018, Ecology and Evolution 8: 8477–8489, Table 1: twelve abandoned kraals vs paired control plots, Save Valley Conservancy, Zimbabwe; aboveground species richness 15.83 vs 9.92, Shannon H′ 1.89 vs 1.62; belowground richness 10.33 vs 5.42, Shannon H′ 1.91 vs 1.25; only belowground diversity significantly higher on kraals

items.notes: Predicate check (Python): richness kraal > control in both strata (5.91, 4.91); Shannon differences 0.66 below vs 0.27 above, ratio 2.44, so “more than twice” holds. B: 15.83 > 10.33 and 1.89 vs 1.91 (accurate, wrong cells). C: 1.62 > 1.25 and 1.89 > 1.62 (accurate, aboveground effect only). D: 5.91 and 4.91 (accurate, richness only). Operations for the key: four reads for richness, two differences for Shannon, one ratio. The claim is phrased in readable differences, not significance. Passage word ‘invertebrates’ follows the paper’s macro-invertebrates.
band7_moves: difference of differences (diversity gap below vs above)
distractors are accurate comparisons of the wrong cells in the key’s frame
passage defines the measure the key depends on (Shannon index) before the claim

items.subtype: Data description: condition vs control with a measure taken before treatment (plots alike beforehand, different afterward)
items.passage: Mangrove forests keep pace with rising sea levels as sediment accumulates among the trees’ roots and the roots add volume to the soil. In a test of small-scale logging, Joseph Lang’at, Mark Huxham, and colleagues killed and then felled the Rhizophora mucronata trees in five plots at Gazi Bay, Kenya, leaving five neighboring plots undisturbed. Beginning months before the trees were killed, they monitored sediment deposition on each plot’s surface and changes in the elevation of the forest floor. The researchers concluded that the treated plots’ loss of elevation resulted from the treatment rather than from differences that already existed between the two sets of plots.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Lang’at and colleagues’ conclusion?
options: Over the study, the surface of the treated plots fell by about 32 millimeters per year, whereas the surface of the control plots rose by about 4 millimeters per year.
Before treatment, the plots that were later treated received about 1.2 millimeters less sediment than the control plots did, which accounts for most of their later loss of elevation.
The top meter of sediment in the treated plots held about 36 fewer metric tons of carbon per hectare than the top meter of sediment in the control plots held.
Before treatment, the two sets of plots received similar amounts of sediment, yet over the study the treated plots’ surface fell about 32 millimeters a year while the control plots’ surface rose.

table.title: Sediment and Surface Elevation in Mangrove Plots at Gazi Bay, Kenya
columns: Treated plots (trees later killed, then cut)
rows: Sediment deposited on surface in first 110 days of monitoring, before treatment (mm)
Average change in surface elevation (mm per year)
Carbon stored in top 1 meter of sediment (metric tons per hectare)

items.explanation: The researchers concluded that the treated plots’ loss of elevation “resulted from the treatment rather than from differences that already existed between the two sets of plots.” To support this, the data must show that the plots were alike before treatment and different afterward. Before treatment, sediment built up at similar rates (5.2 millimeters against 6.4 in the first 110 days), yet over the study the treated plots lost elevation (−32.1 millimeters per year) while the control plots gained it (+4.2). Choice D gives both parts.

A.recipe: PART: the outcome without the pretreatment comparison
A.why_wrong: The elevation figures are accurate and show that the treated plots sank, but without the before-treatment data they cannot rule out that the plots already differed before any trees were killed.

B.recipe: INACC: a real difference made to explain too much
B.why_wrong: The later-treated plots did receive about 1.2 millimeters less sediment in 110 days, but that is about 4 millimeters a year, far too little to account for a gap of more than 36 millimeters a year in elevation change, and it would point to a pre-existing difference, which the researchers reject.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison of a different measure
C.why_wrong: The carbon figures are accurate, but the amount of carbon stored in the sediment does not show whether the plots were alike before treatment or that the treatment caused the loss of elevation.

sources.what: Lang’at, Kairo, Mencuccini, Bouillon, Skov, Waldron, Huxham 2014, PLoS ONE 9(9): e107868: five Rhizophora mucronata plots girdled then cut, five controls, Gazi Bay, Kenya; surface elevation −32.1 mm per year in treated vs +4.2 mm per year in controls over 760 days; sediment accretion in the first 110 days 6.4 mm in controls vs 5.2 mm in treated plots; sediment carbon stocks to 1 m 524.1 vs 488.4 t C per hectare (not significant); subsidence likely due to collapse and decomposition of dying roots and sediment compaction

items.notes: Paper: “For a period of 110 days after setting up the horizon marker, both control and treated plots experienced similar trends in sediment accretion” (6.4 vs 5.2 mm); plots set up March 2009, 760 days of monitoring ending April 2011, girdling October 2009 and cutting May 2010, so the 110-day window falls before treatment (inferred from the stated periods; the paper does not date the marker). ± values (confidence intervals) dropped from the table. ‘Killed’ simplifies girdling. Python: 6.4 − 5.2 = 1.2 mm in 110 days, about 4.0 mm per year; elevation gap 36.3 mm per year; carbon 524.1 − 488.4 = 35.7. Design wrinkle: a measure taken before treatment (band-7 recipe list), written as a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Quotation from a critic supports a student’s interpretive claim (letters used for form rather than meaning)
items.passage: In 1949, Iraqi painter Madiha Omar exhibited twenty-two paintings at a public library in Washington, DC, in which letters of the Arabic alphabet function not as readable text but as shapes distributed across the canvas. That same year, she published a book arguing that Arabic calligraphy could inspire abstract art, and she is now frequently described as a precursor of hurufiyya, a movement of artists who incorporated Arabic letters into modern painting. A student writing about Omar’s work argues that she valued the letters primarily for their visual qualities rather than for their religious associations.
items.stem: Which quotation from an art critic best supports the student’s claim?
options: “The muted browns and ochres of Omar’s backgrounds give her canvases a warmth that sets them apart from the bright, saturated colors favored by many other painters of her generation.”
“Even when Omar’s letters spell nothing at all, they carry the weight of the sacred texts in which Arabic script was perfected, and her paintings invite viewers to recall those texts.”
“Omar freed the letters from their usual task of carrying words, treating their curves, loops, and upright strokes simply as lines and shapes to be balanced on the canvas.”
“Omar’s 1949 exhibition helped introduce audiences in the United States to modern Arab painting at a time when few American galleries showed work by artists from the Middle East.”
items.explanation: The student argues that Omar “valued the letters primarily for their visual qualities rather than for their religious associations.” The critic in choice C says that Omar freed the letters “from their usual task of carrying words,” treating their “curves, loops, and upright strokes simply as lines and shapes to be balanced on the canvas.” That describes letters prized for how they look rather than for what they mean, so choice C supports the assertion.

A.recipe: OFF: describes the paintings, not the use of the letters
A.why_wrong: The quotation discusses the colors of Omar’s backgrounds; it says nothing about why she used Arabic letters.

B.recipe: OPP: argues for the religious reading the student rejects
B.why_wrong: The critic says the letters carry the weight of sacred texts and invite viewers to recall them, which emphasizes their religious associations and so works against the student’s argument.

D.recipe: OFF: the work’s reception, not its approach
D.why_wrong: The quotation concerns the exhibition’s importance for American audiences, not whether Omar valued the letters for their form or for their religious associations.

sources.what: Madiha Omar: in 1949 exhibited 22 hurufist-inspired paintings at Georgetown Public Library in Washington; later in 1949 published Arabic Calligraphy: An Element of Inspiration in Abstract Art; generally perceived as the first Arab artist to use Arabic letters in this way and described as the precursor to the Hurufiyya movement; a 1952 exhibition used Arabic letters in a modern, secular artwork

items.notes: The quotations are from an unnamed art critic, as in official T3 items; they are interpretive, not factual claims about Omar’s life. The student’s assertion rests on the source’s description of her work as modern and secular and of letters used as abstract elements. Wrong options: A OFF (color), B OPP (religious reading), D OFF (reception).

items.subtype: Data description: quantified claim (in each habitat, one lamp type beats every other type measured there)
items.passage: Street lighting in Britain has long used sodium lamps, which produce yellowish light, but local authorities are now replacing them with white light-emitting diodes (LEDs), which emit a broader spectrum of wavelengths. Douglas Boyes and colleagues surveyed moth caterpillars in hedgerows and in grassy road margins in southern England, comparing lit sites with similar unlit sites nearby and noting which type of lamp lit each site. The researchers concluded that the switch to white LEDs is likely to make street lighting more harmful to caterpillars in both of the habitats they studied.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Boyes and colleagues’ conclusion?
options: In both hedgerows and grass margins, lit sites had fewer caterpillars than unlit sites, with an overall reduction of 47% in hedgerows and 33% in grass margins.
In both habitats, the reduction in caterpillars under white LEDs was greater than the reduction under any type of sodium lamp studied in that habitat.
The reduction in caterpillars at sites lit by white LEDs was greater in hedgerows, at 52%, than it was in grass margins, at 43%.
In grass margins, the reduction in caterpillars at sites lit by low-pressure sodium lamps was greater than the reduction at sites lit by high-pressure sodium lamps.

table.title: Reduction in Moth Caterpillars at Lit Sites Compared with Unlit Sites, by Type of Lamp

items.explanation: The researchers concluded that switching to white LEDs is likely to make street lighting “more harmful to caterpillars in both of the habitats they studied.” That requires LED-lit sites to show a larger reduction than sodium-lit sites in each habitat. In hedgerows the reduction was 52% under LEDs against 41% under high-pressure sodium lamps, and in grass margins it was 43% under LEDs against 24% and 11% under the two sodium types. Choice B states this for both habitats.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but pooled over lamp types
A.why_wrong: The overall reductions are accurate, but they combine all lamp types, so they cannot show whether LEDs are more harmful than the sodium lamps they are replacing.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate comparison across the wrong axis (habitat, not lamp)
C.why_wrong: The two LED figures are accurate, but comparing LEDs in one habitat with LEDs in the other says nothing about LEDs versus sodium lamps.

D.why_wrong: In grass margins the reduction under low-pressure sodium lamps, 11%, was smaller than the 24% under high-pressure sodium lamps, and the comparison does not involve LEDs anyway.

sources.what: Boyes, Evans, Fox, Parsons, Pocock 2021, Science Advances 7: eabi8322: matched lit and unlit sites in southern England; hedgerows overall −47%, −52% for LED transects, −41% for HPS; grass margins overall −33%, −43% for LED, −24% for HPS, −11% for LPS; negative impacts more pronounced under white LED street lights than conventional yellow sodium lamps

items.notes: Lamp-specific figures are the paper’s reported effects on abundance. No low-pressure sodium transects were analyzed for hedgerows, so that cell reads ‘not measured’. In grass margins the HPS and LPS effects were not statistically significant; the passage avoids any claim of significance. Python: 52 > 41 (hedgerows), 43 > max(24, 11) (grass margins). The ‘All lamp types’ column feeds distractor A, which matches the habitats but not the lamp comparison.

items.subtype: Data completion: two thresholds stated in the passage applied to signed data (each country meets one but not the other)
items.passage: Among the conditions a European Union member must satisfy before adopting the euro, EU rules establish reference values for public finances: an annual government deficit no greater than 3 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) and government debt no greater than 60 percent of GDP. A deficit is the amount by which government spending exceeds revenue in a particular year, whereas debt is the accumulated total owed from previous borrowing. Figures for 2019, when Bulgaria, Croatia, Hungary, Poland, and Romania were EU members outside the euro, demonstrate that satisfying one reference value does not guarantee satisfying the other: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Croatia and Hungary met the deficit reference value but had debt above 60 percent of GDP, while Romania met the debt reference value but not the deficit one.
Hungary met the reference value for debt, with debt equal to 65.0 percent of GDP, but not the reference value for deficits, since its balance was −2.0 percent of GDP.
Bulgaria and Poland both met the deficit reference value and had debt below 60 percent of GDP, so each met both of the reference values.
Romania met neither reference value, with a deficit of 4.4 percent of GDP and debt of 35.4 percent, while Croatia met both of them.

table.title: Government Balance and Debt of Five EU Countries, 2019
table.note: A negative balance is a deficit; a positive balance is a surplus.

items.explanation: The passage gives the reference values: a deficit of no more than 3 percent of GDP, which means a balance no lower than −3.0, and debt of no more than 60 percent. Croatia (balance 0.1) and Hungary (−2.0) met the deficit value but had debt of 70.6 and 65.0 percent, while Romania’s debt of 35.4 percent was within the limit but its balance of −4.4 was not. Choice A gives countries that met one value and not the other, which is what the statement claims.

B.recipe: WDIR: both thresholds applied the wrong way
B.why_wrong: Hungary’s debt of 65.0 percent is above the 60 percent limit, and its balance of −2.0 percent is a deficit within the 3 percent limit, so Hungary actually met the deficit value and failed the debt value.

C.recipe: TRAP: accurate, but illustrates meeting both
C.why_wrong: Bulgaria and Poland did meet both reference values, but countries that meet both cannot show that meeting one fails to guarantee meeting the other.

D.why_wrong: Romania’s debt of 35.4 percent of GDP was within the 60 percent limit, so it met one value, and Croatia’s debt of 70.6 percent exceeded the limit, so it did not meet both.

sources.what: Eurostat gov_10dd_edpt1, 2019, percent of GDP: net lending (+) / net borrowing (−) B9: BG 2.2, HR 0.1, HU −2.0, PL −0.7, RO −4.4; gross government debt GD: BG 20.1, HR 70.6, HU 65.0, PL 45.2, RO 35.4 (data updated 2026-10-21)

Convergence criteria: government deficit not to exceed 3% of GDP and gross government debt not to exceed 60% of GDP (debt above 60% can comply if sufficiently diminishing, hence ‘reference values’ in the passage)

items.notes: Croatia adopted the euro in 2023 and Bulgaria in 2026; the passage frames the five as not yet in the euro in 2019. Python, deficit test balance ≥ −3.0: BG, HR, HU, PL yes, RO no; debt test ≤ 60: BG, PL, RO yes, HR, HU no. Exactly one option (A) is true and illustrates the claim; C is true but illustrates meeting both. Debt row from the same Eurostat query with na_item=GD.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a single-trait claim (translated novel; hardship treated as ordinary)
items.passage: The Devil’s Pool is an 1846 novel by George Sand, translated by Jane Minot Sedgwick and Ellery Sedgwick. In the novel, Sand characterizes Marie, a poor sixteen-year-old traveling to a distant farm to work as a shepherdess, as treating hunger as a familiar part of life: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from a translation of The Devil’s Pool most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “‘Perhaps,’ she said, ‘but I am too poor. I need at least a hundred crowns to marry, and I must work five or six years to scrape them together.’”
“Oh, I was not hungry; I felt too sad, and I give you my word that even now I have no desire to eat.”
“At first little Marie ate in order to be obliging; then little by little she grew hungry. For, at sixteen, a girl cannot fast for long, and country air is dictatorial.”
“I?—not at all. I am not accustomed like you to four meals a day, and I have been to bed so often without my supper that once more does not trouble me.”
items.explanation: The claim is that Marie treats “hunger as a familiar part of life.” In choice D, Marie says she has “been to bed so often without my supper that once more does not trouble me.” Going without supper is so familiar to her that missing another meal does not bother her, which is what the claim describes.

A.recipe: OFF: same character’s poverty, different subject (saving to marry)
A.why_wrong: Marie says she is too poor to marry and must save for years, but she says nothing about going without meals.

B.recipe: LURE: shares the idea of not eating, for another reason
B.why_wrong: Marie is not hungry because she is sad; she is not treating hunger as a familiar part of her life.

C.why_wrong: The narrator says Marie grows hungry once she starts eating because a girl of sixteen “cannot fast for long,” which does not show her shrugging off a missed meal.

sources.what: George Sand, The Devil’s Pool (La Mare au Diable, 1846), translated by Jane Minot Sedgwick and Ellery Sedgwick (copyright 1894); Marie goes to be a shepherdess at the farms at Ormeaux; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (double hyphen as closed em dash, inner double quotes as single)

items.notes: Single-trait claim at medium, like 2.10 and 2.20; wrong options are the same character’s poverty (A), a keyword lure about not eating (B), and the narrator on her returning appetite (C).

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a two-part claim (travel book; manner outweighs menacing look)
items.passage: A Lady’s Life in the Rocky Mountains is an 1879 travel book by Isabella Bird, made up of letters she wrote while journeying through Colorado in 1873. In the book, Bird recounts her acquaintance with a trapper known as Mountain Jim and conveys that his cultivated conversation led her to look past his menacing appearance: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from A Lady’s Life in the Rocky Mountains most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “‘Desperado’ was written in large letters all over him. I almost repented of having sought his acquaintance.”
“He was very courteous and even kind to me, which was fortunate, as the young men had little idea of showing even ordinary civilities.”
“We entered into conversation, and as he spoke I forgot both his reputation and appearance, for his manner was that of a chivalrous gentleman, his accent refined, and his language easy and elegant.”
“When he’s sober Jim’s a perfect gentleman; but when he’s had liquor he’s the most awful ruffian in Colorado.”
items.explanation: The claim has two parts: Jim’s “cultivated conversation” and the fact that it led Bird “to look past his menacing appearance.” In choice C, Bird says that “as he spoke I forgot both his reputation and appearance,” because “his accent” was “refined” and “his language easy and elegant.” Only this quotation shows his speech making her forget his appearance.

A.why_wrong: Bird describes how threatening Jim looked, but nothing here shows his speech leading her to look past it.

B.why_wrong: Bird praises Jim’s courtesy, but she does not mention his appearance or say that his manner made her overlook it.

D.recipe: LURE: gentleman and ruffian, but a different contrast
D.why_wrong: The quotation contrasts Jim sober and Jim drunk, as judged by someone else; it is not about his speech outweighing his appearance for Bird.

sources.what: Isabella L. Bird, A Lady’s Life in the Rocky Mountains (London: John Murray, 1879), letters from Colorado in 1873; Letter VII, first meeting with “Mountain Jim” (James Nugent) and the host’s verdict; Letter VIII on the ascent of Long’s Peak; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text (inner double quotes as single, straight apostrophes curled)

items.notes: Two-part claim at medium, distractors HALF (A, B) and a keyword lure (D). The claim avoids the wording of official 3.34. The second sentence describing Jim with “a grace of manner which soon made me forget his appearance” was left out because it would also fit the claim.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a claim (local source vs long-distance trade)
items.passage: Dental calculus, the hardened plaque that accumulates on teeth, can trap microscopic particles that a person inhales, including smoke from fires. Analyzing calculus from 67 individuals buried at Bronze Age sites across the eastern Mediterranean, Stephen Buckley and colleagues identified chemical markers of smoke from burning wood and dung at most sites. In individuals from Tiryns, in mainland Greece, and from Chania, on the island of Crete, they also found markers of smoke from lignite, a soft brown coal. The researchers propose that people at each of these two sites obtained lignite from deposits within their own region rather than importing it over long distances.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ proposal?
options: Markers of lignite smoke also appear in the dental calculus of individuals from several other Bronze Age sites in the region dating to the same period.
The chemical signature of the lignite smoke at Tiryns differs from that at Chania, and each matches lignite from deposits in that site’s own region.
Markers of lignite smoke were found in the calculus of both men and women at Tiryns as well as at Chania.
The lignite burned at Tiryns and at Chania came from a single deposit and was carried to both sites by ship.
items.explanation: The researchers propose that people at Tiryns and Chania “obtained lignite from deposits within their own region rather than importing it over long distances.” If the lignite smoke at the two sites has different chemical signatures, each matching deposits in that site’s own region, the lignite at each site came from nearby, so choice B supports the proposal.

A.recipe: OFF: where lignite was burned, not where it came from
A.why_wrong: Lignite smoke at other sites would show that the fuel was used more widely, but it would not show whether the lignite at Tiryns and Chania came from local deposits.

C.why_wrong: Finding lignite smoke in both men and women concerns who was exposed, not the source of the lignite.

D.why_wrong: Lignite shipped from one deposit to both sites would be imported fuel, the opposite of what the researchers propose.

sources.what: Buckley, Power, Andreadaki-Vlazaki et al. 2021, Scientific Reports 11: 24185: dental calculus of 67 individuals from 2nd-millennium BCE Eastern Mediterranean sites; scant combustion markers in Egypt, all other individuals show smoke from wood and/or dung; individuals from Tiryns and Chania also show lignite smoke, consistent with the chemical signature of sources in the northwestern Peloponnese and western Crete respectively; markers in both male and female individuals

items.notes: The key restates as a hypothetical the paper’s own finding (each site’s lignite matches a regional source). C is true in the study but off-target. Medium: one link (distinct regional signatures imply local supply).

items.subtype: Data completion: two pairwise comparisons (a small gap in one country, a large gap in another)
items.passage: Eurostat, the statistical office of the European Union, estimates the average age at which young people in each member country move out of their parents’ household. In 2019, young women in every country listed in the table moved out earlier, on average, than young men did. The magnitude of this difference, however, varied considerably: in certain countries women departed only a few months before men, whereas elsewhere the difference exceeded three years. For example, ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the example?
options: young women in Sweden left home about 12 years earlier, on average, than young women in Croatia did.
in Italy, young men left home about two years earlier, on average, than young women did.
the gap between the ages at which women and men left home was larger in Denmark than in Italy.
in Sweden, women left home less than half a year before men did, whereas in Croatia, women left home 3.5 years before men did.

table.title: Average Age at Which Young People Left the Parental Home, 2019

items.explanation: The example must show that the difference between women and men “varied considerably,” only a few months in some countries and more than three years in others. In Sweden women left home at 17.6 and men at 18.0, a gap of less than half a year, while in Croatia women left at 29.9 and men at 33.4, a gap of 3.5 years. Choice D gives one country of each kind.

A.recipe: IRREL: accurate, but compares women across countries
A.why_wrong: Women in Sweden did leave home about 12 years earlier than women in Croatia, but this compares countries, not the gap between women and men.

B.why_wrong: In Italy young women left home at 29.1 and young men at 31.0, so women, not men, left about two years earlier.

C.why_wrong: The gap was 0.5 years in Denmark and 1.9 years in Italy, so it was smaller in Denmark, not larger.

sources.what: Eurostat yth_demo_030, estimated average age of young people leaving the parental household, 2019: Croatia F 29.9, M 33.4; Denmark F 20.8, M 21.3; Italy F 29.1, M 31.0; Sweden F 17.6, M 18.0 (current release)

items.notes: Python: gaps HR 3.5, DK 0.5, IT 1.9, SE 0.4; women earlier in all four. A: 29.9 − 17.6 = 12.3. Eurostat revises these estimates; values are those of the current release.

items.subtype: Data completion: condition vs control at the same check (grouped bars)
items.passage: Hunters and wildlife managers throughout much of Europe distribute grain and other food at feeding sites to support deer, wild boar, and other game animals. Nuria Selva and colleagues suspected that predators attracted to these sites might also raid the nests of ground-nesting birds in the vicinity. In Poland’s Bieszczady Mountains, the researchers positioned artificial nests containing quail eggs near feeding sites and at control sites more than a kilometer away, then inspected the nests after 6 and 15 days. Nests near feeding sites were raided more frequently: ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?
options: after 6 days, about 52% of the nests near feeding sites had been raided, compared with only about 20% of the nests at control sites.
after 15 days, about 65% of the nests at control sites had been raided, compared with only about 35% of the nests near feeding sites.
about 52% of the nests near feeding sites had been raided after 6 days, and about 65% of them had been raided after 15 days.
after 15 days, about 35% of the nests at control sites had been raided, up from about 20% of those nests after 6 days.

figure.title: Artificial Nests Raided near Feeding Sites and at Control Sites
figure.description: Grouped bar graph with two bars for each check: nests near feeding sites and nests at control sites. Y-axis from 0 to 70 percent. After 6 days: near feeding sites about 52%, control sites about 20%. After 15 days: near feeding sites about 65%, control sites about 35%.

items.explanation: The statement says that “Nests near feeding sites were raided more frequently,” so the completion must compare the two kinds of site at the same check. After 6 days, about 52% of the nests near feeding sites had been raided, against about 20% at control sites. Choice A makes that comparison.

B.recipe: MISPLACED: values swapped between the two groups
B.why_wrong: After 15 days about 65% of the nests near feeding sites, not at control sites, had been raided, and about 35% of the control nests.

C.recipe: PART: one group over time, no control
C.why_wrong: The figures for nests near feeding sites are accurate, but without the control sites they cannot show that those nests were raided more often.

D.recipe: WRONG AXIS: control group over time
D.why_wrong: The control figures are accurate, but comparing the control nests at two checks says nothing about whether nests near feeding sites were raided more often.

sources.what: Selva, Berezowska-Cnota, Elguero-Claramunt 2014, PLoS ONE 9(3): e90740: 120 artificial nests (two Japanese quail eggs each) in feeding and control lines, Bieszczady Mountains, Polish Eastern Carpathians, May 2011; after 6 days 52% of nests near feeding sites vs 20% at control sites depredated; after 15 days 65% vs 35%; control nests 1.7 to 3.7 km from feeding sites

items.notes: Feeding sites in the study are for ungulates (game management). Values are the paper’s means (SDs large). Python: 52 > 20 and 65 > 35, the key gives the day-6 pair.

items.subtype: Data description: change over time (one series rises from below two others to above both and keeps pulling ahead)
items.passage: Research and development (R&D) spending, which finances activities such as laboratory research and the engineering of new products, is commonly measured as a percentage of a country’s gross domestic product (GDP). Examining World Bank data, a student concluded that South Korea, which devoted a smaller share of its economy to R&D than either Japan or Germany did in 2000, subsequently overtook both countries and continued to widen its lead.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the graph that support the student’s conclusion?
options: In 2000, South Korea spent about 2.0% of its GDP on R&D, while Japan spent about 2.9% and Germany spent about 2.4%.
South Korea’s R&D spending rose from about 2.0% of GDP in 2000, below Japan’s and Germany’s, to about 3.7% in 2012, above both, and reached about 4.5% in 2020.
Germany’s R&D spending rose from about 2.4% of GDP in 2000 to about 3.1% in 2020, while Japan’s stayed between about 2.9% and 3.3%.
South Korea’s R&D spending rose in every period shown, while Japan’s and Germany’s fell in every period shown.

figure.title: Research and Development Spending in Three Countries, 2000–2020
figure.description: Three lines for 2000, 2004, 2008, 2012, 2016 and 2020; y-axis from 0 to 5 percent. South Korea: about 2.0, 2.4, 2.9, 3.7, 3.8, 4.5. Japan: about 2.9, 3.0, 3.3, 3.2, 3.1, 3.3. Germany: about 2.4, 2.4, 2.6, 2.8, 2.9, 3.1. South Korea starts below both, passes Germany by 2008 and Japan by 2012, and is far above both in 2020.

items.explanation: The student concluded that South Korea, which spent a smaller share of its economy on R&D than “either Japan or Germany did in 2000, subsequently overtook both countries and continued to widen its lead.” In 2000 South Korea spent about 2.0% of GDP, below Japan’s 2.9% and Germany’s 2.4%; by 2012 it spent about 3.7%, above both, and by 2020 about 4.5%, against roughly 3.3% for Japan and 3.1% for Germany. Choice B describes all three stages.

A.recipe: PART: a single year (the starting gap only)
A.why_wrong: The 2000 figures are accurate, but they show only that South Korea started behind, not that it later overtook Japan and Germany and pulled ahead.

C.recipe: IRREL: accurate trends for the other countries
C.why_wrong: The figures for Germany and Japan are accurate, but without South Korea’s figures they cannot show that South Korea overtook them.

D.recipe: INACC: false claim about two series
D.why_wrong: South Korea’s spending did rise in every period, but Germany’s rose in nearly every period and Japan’s rose from 2000 to 2008 and from 2016 to 2020, so neither fell in every period.

sources.what: World Bank, World Development Indicators, GB.XPD.RSDV.GD.ZS, research and development expenditure (% of GDP): Korea, Rep. 2000 2.049, 2004 2.353, 2008 2.868, 2012 3.685, 2016 3.786, 2020 4.521; Japan 2.858, 2.981, 3.292, 3.174, 3.107, 3.266; Germany 2.387, 2.403, 2.572, 2.825, 2.884, 3.09

items.notes: Replaces the Myanmar subject (claimed first by w4b7_15, withdrawn). Python: Korea < Japan and < Germany in 2000 (2.05 vs 2.86, 2.39); Korea > both in 2012 (3.69 vs 3.17, 2.83) and 2020 (4.52 vs 3.27, 3.09); lead over Japan 0.52 (2012), 0.68 (2016), 1.25 (2020). Germany changes all positive except 2000–2004 (+0.02) so D is false; Japan falls 2008–2012 and 2012–2016 but rises otherwise. Korea passes Germany between 2004 (2.35 vs 2.40) and 2008.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding discriminates between explanations (habitat structure vs prey supply)
items.passage: White-tailed deer have become so abundant in many forests of eastern North America that their browsing eliminates much of the shrub layer and many tree saplings. Comparing fenced plots from which deer had been excluded with neighboring unfenced plots in Pennsylvania and Wisconsin, Elizabeth Roberson, Thomas Rooney, and colleagues found that webs of web-building spiders were about twice as abundant inside the fences. One hypothesis holds that the denser vegetation inside the fences provides spiders with additional structures for anchoring webs; a competing hypothesis holds that fenced plots support more of the flying insects that spiders capture. The researchers concluded that the first hypothesis is more likely.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ conclusion?
options: Spider webs were more abundant in fenced plots than in unfenced plots in both Pennsylvania and Wisconsin.
More flying insects were captured in traps set in the fenced plots than in traps set in the nearby unfenced plots during the same weeks.
Fewer flying insects were available to spiders in fenced plots than in unfenced plots, even though fenced plots held more webs.
In both fenced and unfenced plots, most of the webs were built by spiders belonging to a small number of families.
items.explanation: The researchers concluded that spiders were more abundant inside the fences mainly because the vegetation there “provides spiders with additional structures for anchoring webs,” not because of more prey. If fenced plots actually had fewer flying insects available yet held more webs, more prey cannot explain the difference, which leaves the vegetation hypothesis. Choice C therefore supports the conclusion.

A.why_wrong: More webs inside the fences in both states is the pattern both hypotheses are trying to account for, so it does not favor either.

B.why_wrong: More flying insects inside the fences would support the hypothesis that spiders there had more prey, not the one the researchers favor.

D.recipe: OFF: community makeup, not the cause of abundance
D.why_wrong: Which spider families built the webs says nothing about whether vegetation or prey explains why fenced plots held more webs.

sources.what: Roberson, Chips, Carson, Rooney 2016, PeerJ 4: e2538: paired deer-free (fenced) and control plots, Allegheny Plateau, Pennsylvania, and Northern Highlands, Wisconsin; spider webs twice as abundant in deer-free plots; web scaffold availability 7 to 12 times greater in deer-free plots; prey availability lower in deer-free plots; deer indirectly modify spiders by modifying habitat structure

items.notes: Discrimination check: the scaffold explanation predicts more webs whatever the prey; the prey explanation predicts more prey inside the fences. The key (lower prey inside, the study’s finding; prey was measured in Wisconsin) splits them; A fits both; B is the rival’s prediction. Funnel-web builders (the one family not more abundant in fenced plots) were left out because they would complicate the key.

items.subtype: Data completion: lookup with a two-column filter (region and population)
items.passage: Nunavut, Canada’s largest and northernmost territory, was created in 1999 from the eastern part of the Northwest Territories and is divided into three regions. A student researching communities in Nunavut notes that the territory’s capital, Iqaluit, is located in the Qikiqtaaluk region. According to the table, the community in the Qikiqtaaluk region with fewer than 2,500 residents in 2021 was ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Baker Lake.
Igloolik.
Arviat.
Rankin Inlet.

table.title: Populations of Five Communities in Nunavut, 2021

items.explanation: The statement asks for the community in the Qikiqtaaluk region with fewer than 2,500 residents. The table lists two Qikiqtaaluk communities: Iqaluit, with 7,429 residents, and Igloolik, with 2,049. Igloolik is the one with fewer than 2,500, so choice B is correct.

A.recipe: WRONG GROUP: right size, wrong region
A.why_wrong: Baker Lake had fewer than 2,500 residents (2,061), but it is in the Kivalliq region, not Qikiqtaaluk.

C.recipe: WRONG GROUP: wrong region and size
C.why_wrong: Arviat is in the Kivalliq region and had 2,864 residents.

D.recipe: WRONG GROUP: wrong region and size
D.why_wrong: Rankin Inlet is in the Kivalliq region and had 2,975 residents.

sources.what: Statistics Canada, 2021 Census, population and dwelling counts for Nunavut census subdivisions, as listed: Iqaluit 7,429 (Qikiqtaaluk); Rankin Inlet 2,975, Arviat 2,864, Baker Lake 2,061 (Kivalliq); Igloolik 2,049 (Qikiqtaaluk)

items.notes: Nunavut was created on April 1, 1999, from the eastern Northwest Territories; three regions (Qikiqtaaluk, Kivalliq, Kitikmeot). Filter lookup like 1.12 and 1.40; Baker Lake (2,061) sits just above Igloolik in size but in the wrong region.

items.subtype: Hypothetical finding supports a causal claim (one-step operationalization)
items.passage: Many forest birds choose where to breed in early spring, when they establish territories that they defend through the nesting season. To find out whether people walking in forests disturb birds during this period, Yves Bötsch, Zulima Tablado, and Lukas Jenni had people walk through some forest plots in Switzerland twice a day while birds were establishing territories, leaving other plots undisturbed. The researchers claim that even this low level of human activity caused some birds to settle elsewhere.
items.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support the researchers’ claim?
options: Birds in the disturbed plots fed their young about as often as birds in the undisturbed plots did.
The people who walked through the plots reported seeing a wide variety of bird species.
Birds in the disturbed plots let walkers come closer before flying away than birds in the undisturbed plots did.
By the end of the breeding season, the disturbed plots held about 15 percent fewer bird territories than the undisturbed plots did.
items.explanation: The researchers claim that the walking “caused some birds to settle elsewhere.” If birds avoided settling in the disturbed plots, those plots should end up with fewer territories than the undisturbed ones. Choice D reports exactly that difference, so it supports the claim.

A.why_wrong: How often birds fed their young concerns birds that had already settled, not whether some birds chose to settle elsewhere.

B.why_wrong: Seeing many species says nothing about whether the disturbed plots lost birds to other places.

C.recipe: OPP: birds grew used to walkers
C.why_wrong: Birds letting walkers come closer would suggest they were less bothered by people, which does not support the claim that walking drove birds away.

sources.what: Bötsch, Tablado, Jenni 2017, Proc. R. Soc. B 284: 20170846: forest plots experimentally disturbed by walking through twice a day during territory establishment; number of territories (−15.0%) and species richness (−15.2%) reduced in disturbed plots compared with control plots; low levels of recreation alter settlement decisions

items.notes: Easy one-step operationalization; the key is the study’s headline result. Swiss Ornithological Institute study; plots in Switzerland.

items.subtype: Data completion: maximum in one column (value-only options)
items.passage: Countries near the equator often receive heavy rainfall, but the amount varies widely. A student comparing five tropical countries in Asia, the Pacific, and South America looked up World Bank figures for how much precipitation each country receives in an average year. According to the table, the country with the greatest average annual precipitation is ______
items.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?
options: Colombia.
Papua New Guinea.
Malaysia.
Brunei.

table.title: Average Annual Precipitation in Five Tropical Countries

items.explanation: The statement asks for the country with the greatest average annual precipitation. Colombia receives 3,240 millimeters a year, more than any other country in the table, so choice A is correct.

B.why_wrong: Papua New Guinea receives 3,142 millimeters a year, which is less than Colombia’s 3,240.

C.why_wrong: Malaysia receives 2,875 millimeters a year, less than both Colombia and Papua New Guinea.

D.why_wrong: Brunei receives 2,722 millimeters a year, among the lowest values in the table.

sources.what: World Bank, World Development Indicators, AG.LND.PRCP.MM, average precipitation in depth (mm per year), 2020: Brunei 2,722; Colombia 3,240; Indonesia 2,702; Malaysia 2,875; Papua New Guinea 3,142

items.notes: The indicator is a long-term average (World Bank, from FAO data), reported for 2020. Brunei, Indonesia and Malaysia in Asia, Papua New Guinea in the Pacific, Colombia in South America.

items.subtype: Quotation from a historian supports a claim about an artist’s source (technique from a craft)
items.passage: American artist Ruth Asawa is known for her suspended sculptures of looped wire, which form transparent, interlocking shapes that seem almost weightless. Asawa began making these works in the late 1940s, while she was studying at Black Mountain College in North Carolina. An art history student writing about Asawa argues that the technique she used to construct these sculptures originated in a craft she had observed outside the art world.
items.stem: Which quotation from a work by an art historian would be the most effective evidence for the student to include in support of this claim?
options: “At Black Mountain College, Asawa studied with the painter Josef Albers, who encouraged his students to experiment with ordinary, inexpensive materials found in everyday life.”
“Asawa’s sculptures are often hung in groups, so that the shadows they cast on nearby walls and floors become part of the work.”
“During a visit to Toluca, Mexico, in the 1940s, Asawa watched local craftspeople loop wire into baskets for carrying eggs, and she adapted their method for her sculptures.”
“Later in her career, Asawa designed several public fountains in San Francisco and worked to bring professional artists into the city’s schools.”
items.explanation: The student argues that Asawa’s technique “originated in a craft she had observed outside the art world.” The historian in choice C says that Asawa watched craftspeople in Toluca, Mexico, “loop wire into baskets for carrying eggs” and “adapted their method for her sculptures.” Basket making is a craft outside the art world, so choice C supports the claim.

A.recipe: OFF: an influence from within the art world
A.why_wrong: Albers was a painter and teacher at an art school, and the quotation concerns materials rather than the looping technique, so it does not show the technique came from a craft outside the art world.

B.recipe: OFF: how the work is displayed
B.why_wrong: The quotation describes how the sculptures are hung and the shadows they cast, not where Asawa’s technique came from.

D.why_wrong: Designing fountains and supporting arts education are later parts of Asawa’s career and say nothing about the source of her wire technique.

sources.what: Ruth Asawa: in 1947, while at Black Mountain College (1946 to 1949, studying with Josef Albers, who taught use of commonplace materials), made looped-wire sculptures using a wire-looping technique learned from craftspeople in Toluca, Mexico, inspired by market baskets for eggs and produce; later public fountains in San Francisco (the ‘fountain lady’) and the Alvarado Arts Workshop bringing artists into schools

items.notes: Quotations are from an unnamed historian, as in official T3 items; the key states the documented Toluca origin, kept to ‘the 1940s’ because sources date the trip 1945 or 1947.

items.subtype: Literary quotation illustrates a single-trait claim (poem; delight in the stormy sea)
items.passage: “December in Scituate” is an 1899 poem by Bliss Carman. While visiting a friend’s seaside house, the speaker takes considerable delight in the stormy winter sea: ______
items.stem: Which quotation from “December in Scituate” most effectively illustrates the claim?
options: “All summer here the crooning winds / Are cradled in the rocking dunes, / Till they, full height and burly grown, / Go seaward and forget their croons.”
“I could sit here all day and watch / The seas at battle smoke and wade, / And in the cold night wake to hear / The booming of their cannonade.”
“Here is the slanting open field, / Where billow upon billow rolls / The sea of daisies in the sun, / When June brings back the orioles.”
“And now, ten minutes from the train, / Over the right-hand easy swell, / We catch the sparkle of the sea / And the green roof of Tortoise Shell.”
items.explanation: The claim is that the speaker “takes considerable delight in the stormy winter sea.” In choice B he says, “I could sit here all day and watch / The seas at battle,” and that in “the cold night” he wakes “to hear / The booming of their cannonade.” Wanting to watch the battling waves all day shows his delight in the stormy winter sea.

A.recipe: OFF: summer winds, not the stormy winter sea
A.why_wrong: These lines describe the summer winds over the dunes, not the speaker enjoying the stormy sea in winter.

C.recipe: LURE: ‘billow’ and ‘sea’ used for a field of flowers
C.why_wrong: The “sea” here is a field of daisies in June, so the lines are not about the stormy winter sea.

D.recipe: OFF: a first glimpse of the sea on arrival
D.why_wrong: The speaker only catches “the sparkle of the sea” as he arrives; he does not describe a stormy sea or how much he enjoys it.

sources.what: Bliss Carman, A Winter Holiday (Boston: Small, Maynard & Company, 1899), poem “December in Scituate”; all four quotations checked as exact substrings of the Gutenberg text

items.notes: Easy single-trait claim; the key is the one stanza that joins the stormy sea and the speaker’s pleasure in it. Scituate is in Massachusetts; ‘Tortoise Shell’ is the friend’s house.

items.subtype: Data description: two treatments vs control on the measure the conclusion names
items.passage: In integrated rice-frog farming, frogs are raised in flooded rice paddies, where they eat insect pests. Kaikai Fang and colleagues compared two rice-frog systems with conventional farming, which uses chemical fertilizer only, in fields near Shanghai, China: one rice-frog system used equal amounts of chemical and organic fertilizer, and the other used organic fertilizer only. For each system, the team measured how much rice was grown and the global warming potential, an estimate of the combined warming effect of the greenhouse gases a field releases. The researchers concluded that both rice-frog systems had a greater warming effect than conventional farming did.
items.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support Fang and colleagues’ conclusion?
options: Global warming potential was about 141% of the conventional level for the half-organic rice-frog system and about 198% for the organic-only system.
Rice yield in the organic-only rice-frog system was about 7,351 kilograms per hectare, the lowest yield of the three systems.
The half-organic rice-frog system produced nearly as much rice as conventional farming did, about 8,650 kilograms per hectare compared with about 8,828.
Global warming potential was lower for the organic-only rice-frog system than it was for the half-organic rice-frog system.

table.title: Rice Yield and Global Warming Potential of Three Farming Systems
columns: Global warming potential (% of conventional farming)

items.explanation: The researchers concluded that “both rice-frog systems had a greater warming effect than conventional farming did.” Global warming potential was 141% of the conventional level for the half-organic system and 198% for the organic-only system, both above conventional farming’s 100%. Choice A gives these figures.

B.why_wrong: The organic-only system did have the lowest yield, but rice yield is not the warming effect the conclusion is about.

C.why_wrong: The yield figures are accurate, but they say nothing about whether the rice-frog systems had a greater warming effect.

D.why_wrong: The organic-only system’s global warming potential, 198%, was higher, not lower, than the half-organic system’s 141%.

sources.what: Fang, Yi, Dai, Gao, Cao 2019, Int. J. Environ. Res. Public Health 16(11): 1930: randomized plots at the Modern Agricultural Park of Qingpu, Shanghai, 2018; CF (full chemical fertilizer), GIRF (50% chemical and 50% organic fertilizer, with frogs), OIRF (100% organic fertilizer, with frogs); rice yields 8,827.56, 8,650.38 and 7,350.69 kg per hectare (2.0% and 16.7% below CF); GWP increased by 41.3% (GIRF) and 98.2% (OIRF) over CF

items.notes: GWP shown relative to conventional farming (100 + 41.3 and 100 + 98.2, rounded), since the paper gives whole-season GWP as percentage increases. The conclusion is worded as the systems’ effect, not the frogs’ (the paper attributes most of the methane to fertilization). Yields rounded to the kilogram.
